inserts.title: Perspective correction fixes the error reference
paragraphs: Overhead video shows a falling prey at positions that shift with its height, because camera perspective changes as the object descends. Rossel and colleagues corrected that perspective for the prey's changing height before any error was scored. The correction treated the water surface as the reference plane, so each landing estimate was read in one physical frame.

Without that correction, the image position of a falling prey would drift as the object fell, and errors would be scored against a moving reference. Destinations for the 20 and 40 cm release heights were therefore placed on the same error scale, which makes the two heights directly comparable. Each landing estimate kept its meaning at either height.

Overhead video sampled prey and fish positions at 20-ms intervals. Temporal resolution sets the precision assigned to each individual response latency, so every latency value is an estimate tied to that frame interval. Latencies are therefore reported as estimates at the resolution of that frame interval. The sampling rate therefore sets how precisely any turn onset can be dated.
notes: Perspective correction fixes the error reference.

Overhead video shows a falling prey at positions that shift with its height, because camera perspective changes as the object descends

Rossel and colleagues corrected that perspective for the prey's changing height before any error was scored. The correction treated the water surface as the reference plane, so each landing estimate was read in one physical frame.

Explanation 3.

inserts.title: Within-trial errors isolate the early aim
paragraphs: Both error measures came from the same responses within each trial. Because one group of fish and one stimulus history supplied both measures, the contrast between the two errors is free of differences between animal groups or stimulus histories. The within-trial design keeps the aim measure tied to a single set of turns. Each trial supplied both values.

Prediction could operate through an explicit internal trajectory or through a learned relation between sensory variables and the destination. Measured errors identify where the fish aimed, whereas the internal computation behind that aim is a separate question. The data therefore constrain the output of the computation without naming its form. Each interpretation predicts a different pattern across trials.

Eventual catches alone would be weaker evidence, because the initial heading exists before later corrections take effect. Subsequent swimming corrections change the path after the fact, so the early heading is the record that reflects the fish's estimate before the outcome is known. A fish with a learned relation would show the same early aim across repeated trials of one stimulus.
notes: Within-trial errors isolate the early aim.

Both error measures came from the same responses within each trial

Because one group of fish and one stimulus history supplied both measures, the contrast between the two errors is free of differences between animal groups or stimulus histories. The within-trial design keeps the aim measure tied to a single set of turns. Each trial supplied both values.

inserts.title: Kinematics describe the movement, not its commands
paragraphs: The silhouette sequence is the authors' published high-speed record, with stage colors and measured center-of-mass markers that follow the body through both stages. Predictive starts were filmed from above, so the silhouettes show the turn in the horizontal plane. Each silhouette is an original frame from the recording rather than a drawing. Those markers track each stage in order.

A kinematic record specifies the form and timing of a start. Identifying the descending neurons that initiate the maneuver calls for separate measurements, because the movement itself carries no label for its source. Experiments that record or stimulate the command pathway provide evidence that the body record alone lacks. Such experiments can separate the two possibilities directly.

The two-stage sequence repeats across starts, so the bending stage serves as a consistent marker of when the turn is being set. Each start was resolved frame by frame at 2-ms intervals, which keeps the stage boundaries explicit in the analysis. Stage boundaries defined this way give every start a shared timing reference for analysis.
notes: Kinematics describe the movement, not its commands.

inserts.title: Bending predicts turns, not commands
paragraphs: The original relation compares the required turn angle with the extent of body bending, so each start contributes a paired measurement of the two. Those pairs spanned the whole range of turns in the recordings. Each pair links one observed start to the turn it needed to complete. The relation therefore tracks turn size against bending extent.

Correlations among body measurements show which features vary together, while the order in which the nervous system specifies those features is a separate question. A correlation can rank features by how tightly they track each other without revealing which one is set first. Establishing that order requires experiments that manipulate the features directly. Such a ranking is descriptive.

A kinematic predictor is useful because it links a measurable body shape to the turn the fish is about to complete. That link gives experimenters a quantity they can measure in every start before the turn is finished. Measuring the bending stage therefore offers an early readout of the turn's final angle. Its value is in timing.
notes: Bending predicts turns, not commands.

inserts.title: Rare misses expose the jet beyond its target
paragraphs: Missed short-range targets supplied the uninterrupted jets needed for this comparison. The shaft comparison therefore used jets that reached the common 30-cm path without being interrupted by a target. Each jet was examined at the same travel distance, which made the shaft shape directly comparable across intended ranges. This design kept travel distance constant across the jets.

Because every shaft was examined after the same travel distance, differences in shaft shape reflect the intended range rather than a difference in path length. The design therefore reads the same measurement across all three target heights. Shaft modulation is a property of the emitted water itself, observed after release. Shaft shape therefore carries the range information.

Each shot contributes one shaft image tied to one intended range, which gives a direct record of the jet's coherence at that range. Those records were gathered for the same set of shooting heights used in the focusing images. The shaft records therefore complement the focusing images collected for the same heights, giving two views of one shot.

inserts.title: Measured fluid properties match control water
paragraphs: Shot viscosity was 0.867 mPa·s, against 0.869 mPa·s for control water. Surface tension was 70.37 mN/m for the shot water and 70.49 mN/m for the control, so the two fluids were nearly identical in both measures. The shot water was collected directly from the fish's own shots, so the values describe the fluid the fish actually emitted.

The fluid properties were measured for shots aimed at several target heights. Neither viscosity nor surface tension changed systematically with the intended range, which fits a fixed fluid composition across the shots. Chemical tuning of the jet would have required one of these properties to vary with range. The fish's emission was sampled at each height.

Mouth-tip drift and body rotation were measured during the same emission period, and neither changed systematically with target height. Those movements were small enough that the water release itself carried the range difference. The jet's range was therefore set inside the mouth rather than by the fish's body position. Mouth measures are therefore central to the range question.
notes: Measured fluid properties match control water.

inserts.title: Receptor curves keep their original scales
paragraphs: The regional spectra are drawn from curves that keep their original axes and relative sensitivity scales. Each curve shows how absorption changes with wavelength in one selected photoreceptor, so the shapes can be compared across retinal locations. The published figure keeps every curve in its original form. Each spectrum therefore has its own scale and baseline.

The retina's two regions view different parts of the environment, and the spectral curves show how each region samples light from them. The aquatic and aerial views therefore carry different light conditions into the eye, and each region's spectrum reflects the light it receives. The curves therefore reflect the light each region receives. Each region's sensitivity is measured directly.

Spectral coverage is a property of the receptors themselves, so it sets which wavelengths are available for detecting a target against the sky. Spectral and spatial measures are therefore reported separately for each retinal region, so each region's capabilities can be read on its own terms. A region with broad coverage can respond to more contrasts than a narrow one.
notes: Receptor curves keep their original scales.

inserts.title: Relative timing references the population, not the motor act
paragraphs: Relative latencies are referenced to the onset of the recorded population response, not to the animal's motor response. The reference therefore belongs to the retinal recording itself, which is distinct from when the fish decides to move. This reference makes the timing measure depend on the recorded responses alone. That choice keeps the analysis focused on the responses themselves.

The four decoding analyses were the authors' own original analysis of the same recorded responses. Each ranking of decoders is therefore a comparison made on one dataset rather than on separate experiments. A shared dataset makes the difference between decoders a difference in method rather than in the animals sampled. The shared dataset keeps every ranking on equal footing.

A spike-count estimate integrates activity over a longer period, so a short first-spike window can carry information that a count over a longer window would average out. The first-spike analysis uses that early timing directly. Its advantage lies in using the earliest spikes that the cell produces after onset. That choice favors the earliest information in each response.

inserts.title: Analytical filters describe the response model
paragraphs: The published eigenvectors belong to an analytical response model, which describes how the neuron responds to light history. They are not a reconstructed anatomical circuit, so each filter stands for a computation rather than a wiring diagram. Each eigenvector is a weighting over the preceding light levels, read off the fitted model. The fitted model defines each weighting directly.

Reichenthal and colleagues used full-field flashes, so every filter describes responses to a whole-field light history rather than to a spatial pattern. The temporal analysis therefore complements the earlier receptive-field maps. Spatial and temporal structure were measured with separate stimulus sets, so each dimension could be analyzed separately. Each dimension therefore has its own measurement basis.

The filters are estimated from the stimuli presented and the amount of recorded activity, so their precision follows the data collected. Larger recordings would give the same analysis more samples to estimate each filter. Filter estimates therefore improve as the recorded activity grows. Estimates from short recordings carry more variability than those from long ones.
notes: Analytical filters describe the response model.

inserts.title: The axon cap shapes the field signal
paragraphs: The focused extracellular signal depends on the geometry of the axon cap around the cell, which shapes where the field is strongest. That geometry means the signal reports the cell's local field rather than an average over the hindbrain. Field recordings near the cell therefore identify a particular neuron's signal. The cell's geometry therefore shapes each recording.

Antidromic stimulation travels backward from axon toward cell body, so it activates the cell by way of its axon. That route is distinct from the forward flow of sensory input through the dendrites. Stimulation of this kind is an experimental probe rather than a description of natural input. Its route bypasses the dendritic inputs that carry natural sensory signals.

Antidromic activation shows that the cell can be driven from its axon, a property separate from its firing during a natural prey-directed turn. Experimental access to that axon is what makes the cell testable in the first place. The identified cell then serves as a platform for the sensory tests that follow. That identification makes the cell a usable target.
notes: The axon cap shapes the field signal.

inserts.title: The distant reference carries the spike field
paragraphs: The distant reference can itself carry the local spike-associated field, which is why the external potential has to be corrected before the membrane voltage is determined. The correction turns a reference reading into an estimate of the cell's own voltage. Without it, the spike seen at a distant electrode would mix the cell's voltage with the surrounding field.

Each intracellular spike was checked against the field recorded around the cell, so the reported spike amplitude belongs to the cell rather than to its surroundings. This isolates the cell's own voltage change from the surrounding potential. The distinction matters for every amplitude value reported for these neurons. Each spike amplitude was therefore corrected before analysis.

Stable recordings allowed the same cell to be tested with repeated stimulation over the course of an experiment. Because the excitability measures come from one identified neuron, each response can be judged within that cell. Repeated tests in one cell make paired comparisons possible. Each recording therefore yields several measures from a single neuron. That reuse is a practical advantage of the preparation.
notes: The distant reference carries the spike field.

inserts.title: Two dendritic sites bracket the lateral dendrite
paragraphs: Recordings were made about 50 and 150 µm lateral to the axon hillock, giving a proximal and a distal site on the same lateral dendrite. The two positions bracket the region where the sensory inputs were compared. Passive spread is the common basis for interpreting both positions. Both sites sit on the same dendrite, so they share one geometry.

The gradient interpretation relies on passive decay measured independently, so the spread of each input is set by the cell's own passive properties. That independent measurement anchors the reading of the two gradients. A reading of that kind depends on knowing the passive decay before the inputs are interpreted. Passive decay sets how far a voltage change spreads along the dendrite.

Anatomical tracing of each presynaptic axon is a separate task from measuring these gradients. Gradient measurements locate the likely entry region of an input, while tracing identifies the axon that carries it. The two approaches answer different questions about the same synapse. Tracing would name the carrying axon directly, something gradient measures alone never supply.

paragraphs: Airflow acted on the aerial water stream, while the target location remained under experimental control. The airflow therefore changed the jet's path without changing where the visible target sat. Errors came from the stream itself, which is why the setup isolates the deflection of the jet. The stream itself was the object of the deflection in every trial.

The published setup includes a photographed water jet, which documents the stream that the airflow deflects. That image anchors the stream geometry that the blower acted on. The photographed jet is the physical object whose deflection the fish corrected across the session. The photograph therefore links the apparatus to the jet that the fish aimed, which helps interpret the errors.

Adjustment was tested in both directions, so the correction could be checked for whether it worked for either direction of deflection. Each direction was run as its own condition in the same session. Those conditions show whether the fish's adjustment worked on one side or on both. Both airflow directions were therefore run in every session.

inserts.title: Virtual prey separate the rule from the feeder
paragraphs: The virtual task keeps an objective predicted landing point while letting the investigators change the motion-to-reward relation. That arrangement allows the reward to follow a rule that a physical falling prey could not supply. The prediction stays fixed while the reward moves, which isolates the learning from the physical scene. This setup gives the experimenter direct control of reward timing and location.

Latency and accuracy were reported together across the training sequence, so the speed of the predictive start and its correctness both show how the learned rule developed. The two measures tracked each other as training progressed. Together they show the rule emerging without a change in the response's speed. Both measures are summarized across the same trials.

Rapid decisions persisted while the learned rule changed, which places the plasticity inside the speed constraint of the start. The change therefore affects which destination is chosen without slowing the response into a deliberate approach. The learned rule thus operates within the same fast motor program. The speed of the response was preserved throughout training.
notes: Virtual prey separate the rule from the feeder.

2: Archerfish are aquatic predators that dislodge aerial prey with a **directed water jet**. In Toxotes jaculatrix, a successful shot releases an insect into a falling trajectory, and the fish then has to reach the water-entry point before a rival does. The landing site sets the race, since the first fish to reach it secures the food.

Rossel and colleagues recorded fish and dislodged flies from above. Responding fish began a rapid turn within about 100 ms, aligned toward the future landing point, and accelerated along that heading while the prey remained airborne. Shooting and interception therefore impose different motor demands. Each fish therefore solved a moving interception problem in midair.

Gerullis and Schuster recorded shots at controlled target heights of 20, 40 and 60 cm. Those experiments measured jet control and prey interception directly, so each behavior can be analyzed on its own terms before the neurons behind it are identified. The jet and the interception data describe complementary halves of one foraging sequence.
3: A **ballistic trajectory** is motion dominated by initial velocity and gravity after release. Rossel and colleagues dropped wet flies of about 50 mg from a disk positioned 20 or 40 cm above the water, and overhead video tracked prey and fish positions throughout each trial. Each release therefore set a predictable path for the prey to follow.

The investigators measured each error against two possible destinations. One was the eventual water-entry point, and the other was the prey's horizontal position when the fish finished turning. Scoring errors against both targets identifies which destination the turn was aimed at. Aiming at the landing point means predicting, while aiming at the visible position means pursuing.

Trials with obstructed turns were excluded from the analysis. Initial misalignment had to exceed 10 degrees so that the start and end of each turn could be identified, and those criteria kept responses whose timing could be measured. Those criteria kept the analysis focused on clean, measurable turns that the video could resolve.
4: Released flies landed farther away as their initial horizontal velocity increased. Rossel and colleagues compared the measured landing distances at release heights of 20 and 40 cm with published ballistic predictions, and the two sets agreed closely. Landing distance therefore changed systematically with the conditions at release, in each tested case. Both release heights were measured directly.

The agreement held under the assumptions of negligible air resistance and negligible initial vertical velocity. Under those conditions, the landing point depends on horizontal speed and release height, which together set how long the fly stays airborne. The tested approximation describes how these physical quantities combine to set the landing point. The landing relation was measured, not presumed.

The same horizontal speed produces a more distant landing point at greater height, because a higher object remains airborne for longer. A fish must therefore combine motion information with height information to find the destination. Ballistic motion makes this dependence predictable, since the trajectory follows directly from release velocity and height. Height adds airtime.
5: A bystander's starting orientation can differ widely from the direction in which a dislodged fly moves. Rossel and colleagues sampled this relation at both 20 and 40 cm prey heights, including starts that required large turns before acceleration toward the destination. Such orientations appeared across the sampled responses at both heights, including the extreme cases.

Responders therefore translated prey motion into a body-centered turning requirement from many positions and orientations in the tank. Turning generally finished before the prey entered the water, so the turn was complete while the prey was still airborne. Turning requirements were computed from the prey's motion rather than from the fish's own starting direction.

The range of turn sizes makes a fixed turn angle an inadequate explanation of interception. The analysis included unobstructed first responders, so the measured turns describe the earliest fish to reach each falling prey. Each measured turn therefore reflects the heading chosen by one first responder for one falling prey, in one trial.
6: Rossel and colleagues measured where each fish's final heading intersected the prey's projected horizontal path. In critical tests that displayed the early straight trajectory alone, feeders were moved away from both candidate impact points, and fish still aimed at the learned deflected point. Turns continued toward the learned point even though the feeders had moved away from both candidates.

The response remained a rapid predictive start rather than a slow approach. This establishes plasticity in the link between early motion and chosen destination, while the storage site of that rule is a separate question. Immediate acquisition of the rapid response indicates that learning changed the decision itself, not only movement timing.
43: Krause and colleagues tested whether learning simply replaced familiar stimulus-response associations. Fish trained at one height were challenged at other heights, where the old training-height response and the new rule predicted different destinations. The old response and the new rule thus pointed to different locations, so a choice between them was measurable.

Initial turns were already appropriate for the untrained heights rather than systematically approaching the training-height substitute. Additional tests changed object size and included an untrained speed of 1.425 m/s, and the learned relation **generalized** beyond the exact combinations used during training. Object size and speed were varied, so the rule had to hold across changed conditions.

Immediate transfer supports a more general representation than a lookup list restricted to trained cases. The interpretation rests on the competing predicted destinations in these controlled transfer trials, rather than on equating a successful catch with abstract reasoning. A learned rule that applies to new combinations is more useful than a memorized list of trials.
44: Krause and colleagues trained fish with two visually different prey objects. A disk required the learned deflected relation, whereas a triangle required the original ballistic relation. Shape and initial motion were controlled, so the same motion variables could require different destinations. Prey shape therefore served as the cue that identified which rule applied.

In interspersed tests, the initial trajectory alone was visible. Fish directed turns toward the deflected virtual point for disks and the ballistic virtual point for triangles, so the decision could use a **context cue** to choose between two concurrent motion-to-destination relations. Shape cues therefore gave the fish a reliable basis for choosing the destination.

This is stronger evidence than learning one fixed turn toward each shape, because required turns also depended on prey speed, direction, height and fish position. Identifying the cells that recognize the object and the synapses that switch the motor computation is a separate task. Speed, direction and height all shaped the required turns in these trials.
45: Krause and colleagues tested whether a shape cue had to appear before prey motion to prepare the right decision. A neutral cross stayed stationary for 2 seconds, then changed into the relevant disk or triangle exactly when movement began. The late-cue condition therefore tested choice timing against an early-cue condition. The cue timing was controlled exactly.

Just the initial straight movement was displayed, so the later deflection gave no information about the correct destination. Errors were comparable to those obtained when object identity had been visible 2 seconds before motion, and the fish selected the **appropriate rule** during the brief decision interval itself. Both conditions produced accurate rule selection.

This finding adds conditional flexibility to a response made in less than 100 ms under the tested conditions. Together with the transfer tests, it constrains simple accounts of a fixed reflex, while the circuitry for visual recognition and command selection is a topic for later investigation. The behavior occurred within the response window, so decisions were made in midflight.
